name: Bottle green
lede: Bottle green is the dark green of glass bottles, a name in use by the 1820s and later fixed on colour charts as a blue-leaning green.

sections.title: A glass color
sections.body:
Paterson defines *bottle green* as the dark green of some wine bottles, and also as a dark yellowish green [1]. He keeps it apart from *Coke bottle green*, the distinctive green of Coca-Cola bottles, which has its own entry [1]. The name is an object word, so it never meant one exact color: bottles vary with the glass.

In printed English the phrase peaks in the 1820s, though the count includes any use of the words, not only the color [2].

sections.title: A stage in the dye vat
sections.body:
Dyers knew the color as a sign. In a dyeing recipe from William Partridge's 1823 treatise, as Garfield reports it, a woad-and-indigo vat set in the afternoon should be bottle-green by that evening, after which the dyer lightens it with lime or more indigo [3]. The color served as a check that the vat was working, long before the cloth came out blue.

The word also turns up in painting. St Clair describes the gown in the Arnolfini Portrait, dated 1434, as bottle-green [4]. By her account a deep, even green was costly, because it needed two dye baths, first woad and then weld [4]. Her description, not a measurement, is the source for the word here.

sections.title: The swatch is bluer than the bottle
sections.body:
The swatch comes from color charts, not from glass. Our library traces it to Ridgway's 1886 *Nomenclature of Colors*, carried over to his 1912 plate XIX, and to Maerz and Paul in 1930 [5]. The ISCC-NBS system of 1955 files it under block 138 and calls the nearest named region a moderate green, 6.6 CIEDE2000 units away [5]. The chart color is a clear blue-green, while Paterson's second sense is yellowish [1][5]. Compare [[emerald-green]].

So the name fits two greens.

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body: The color is rare in paint. In our archive of 23,781 paintings, a color within six units of this swatch covers at least five per cent of the canvas in only 6 works [6]. The earliest is Davies's *Ship in Full Sail* of 1827, and the others run to 1929 [6]. Half of those appearances are the darkest tones of their pictures [6]. These are photographs of varnished paintings, so read them as screen colors, not pigments [6].

choices: That the vat was too hot
That it was ready to drain

questions.q: Which two dyes made a deep green in a two-bath process?

openers: Dyers once watched a woad-and-indigo vat turn bottle-green to know it was working.
The Arnolfini gown is called bottle-green by one author, and it needed two dye baths.

issues: Recipe was Partridge 1823 (Garfield), not eighteenth century; vat was woad-and-indigo, timing 'that evening'.
